content: 1. Ethinylestradiol reduces the effectiveness of ursodiol through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Close monitoring is advised when these medications are used together. 2. Vadadustat increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol through mechanisms not fully detailed. Caution and close monitoring are recommended. 3. Vadadustat may increase the exposure of substrates of the Breast Cancer Resistance Protein (BCRP). Monitor for adverse effects related to BCRP substrates and adjust the substrate dose as per their product labeling. 4. Both ethinylestradiol and valoctocogene roxaparvovec can increase certain effects (details unspecified). Use caution and monitor closely. 5. Medications that may cause hepatotoxicity, when combined with valoctocogene roxaparvovec, could elevate the risk of increased liver enzyme levels. These medications should be closely monitored, and alternative therapies should be considered if drug interactions are likely. 6. Ethinylestradiol decreases the levels or effects of valproic acid by increasing its elimination. This interaction may lead to an increased frequency of seizures. Therapy modification and close monitoring are necessary. 7. Voriconazole increases the levels or effects of ethinylestradiol by inhibiting hepatic and intestinal CYP3A4 enzyme metabolism. Caution and close monitoring are advised. 8. Common side effects of ethinylestradiol include emotional instability, headaches, abdominal pain, nausea, breast symptoms, menstrual cramps, and application site reactions. Serious risks include arterial or venous thromboembolism, hypertension, myocardial infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, gallbladder disease, hepatic adenomas, and dysgeusia. 9. Ethinylestradiol is contraindicated in individuals with documented hypersensitivity, active or past breast cancer, arterial thromboembolic disease (e.g., stroke, myocardial infarction), thrombophlebitis, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE), thrombotic valvular disease, estrogen-dependent neoplasia, liver disease or tumors, undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding, uncontrolled hypertension, or diabetes mellitus with vascular involvement. 10. Discontinue ethinylestradiol if jaundice, visual problems (e.g., contact lens intolerance), signs of venous thromboembolism (VTE), unusually severe migraines, significant blood pressure increases, or severe depression develop. 11. Ethinylestradiol should be discontinued at least four weeks before major surgery or prolonged immobilization to reduce the risk of thromboembolic complications. 12. Patients on warfarin or other oral anticoagulants may require an increased anticoagulant dose when using ethinylestradiol. 13. Some studies suggest an increased risk of breast cancer with oral contraceptive (OCP) use, while others do not show a change in risk. Risk factors include early menarche (before age 12), late menopause (after age 55), first childbirth after age 30, and nulliparity. 14. Long-term OCP use (five or more years) may be associated with an increased risk of cervical cancer, although human papillomavirus (HPV) remains the primary risk factor. 15. OCP use is associated with an increased risk of liver cancer, with the risk rising with longer durations of use. 16. The risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) is highest during the first year of OCP use and may increase when combined hormonal contraceptives are restarted after a break of four weeks or longer. 17. The CDC recommends waiting at least three weeks after vaginal birth or six weeks after cesarean section before initiating combined hormonal contraceptives to reduce the risk of VTE. Women with additional VTE risk factors should avoid combined hormonal contraceptives. 18. Ethinylestradiol is classified as Pregnancy Category X and should not be used during pregnancy. 19. Small amounts of steroids are excreted in breast milk, and estrogens may reduce the quality and quantity of milk. Alternative birth control methods are recommended until full weaning. However, the AAP Committee considers ethinylestradiol compatible with nursing. 20. Ethinylestradiol suppresses the release of luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) from the hypothalamus and gonadotropin release from the pituitary. It also increases the synthesis of DNA, RNA, and various proteins in target tissues. 21. Norelgestromin, a progestin, inhibits gonadotropin secretion from the pituitary, prevents follicular maturation and ovulation, and stimulates mammary tissue growth. 22. The half-life of ethinylestradiol is approximately 17 hours, while that of norelgestromin is about 28 hours. 23. Norelgestromin is metabolized into norgestrel, its primary metabolite. 24. Ethinylestradiol has a bioavailability of approximately 60% and is excreted via urine and feces. 25. Formulary information for medications can be compared by creating a list of plans.
